title: The Gold Card
summary:
The White House has created a new immigration pathway called the Gold Card. It offers a faster route to a U.S. immigrant visa for people who make a large financial gift to the Department of Commerce—$1 million for an individual, or $2 million if a company donates on someone’s behalf.

The stated goal is to align immigration with national interests by prioritizing entrants who can contribute to the economy. The donation will be treated as evidence that the applicant benefits the country and has exceptional business ability, helping them qualify for certain employment-based green card categories and a “national interest” waiver. The money will go into a dedicated fund to promote American industry. Agencies have 90 days to set up the application process, fees for expedited handling, and a start date. Companies can sponsor a person and later transfer that sponsorship to a different individual, subject to security checks. Officials may also consider expanding the program to investor visas, all within existing visa limits under law.

Who stands to benefit? Wealthy entrepreneurs and investors seeking permanent residency could gain a faster, clearer path. U.S. companies may get a new tool to attract global talent. The Commerce Department and related programs could see fresh funding, and some communities could benefit if donations translate into projects that support jobs and industry.

Who might be negatively affected? People without deep financial resources could see this as a “pay to immigrate” system that favors the rich over applicants waiting in traditional backlogs. It could raise fairness and ethics concerns, and critics may worry about the message it sends about access to residency. There may also be questions about oversight, potential abuse, and how this interacts with existing visa caps and long-standing pathways.

In short, the Gold Card aims to trade speed for sizable donations, with promised economic gains—and a likely debate about equity and priorities in the immigration system.
